solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Children not keen on first part of The Four Seasons

parts.note: to be off something is to have gone off it, no longer liking it

parts.words: first part of The Four Seasons
parts.note: Vivaldi's The Four Seasons opens with the concerto for spring

explanation.surface: Someone's kids can't stand the opening movement of Vivaldi's famous work.
explanation.definitionFit: Offspring are a person's descendants, their children, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Fruit cultivated in Gerona

indicators.note: cultivated soil is worked over, so the letters are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: Citrus grown around the Spanish city of Gerona.
explanation.definitionFit: An orange is a citrus fruit, an example of the category.

clue.text: Aggressive action causing alarm? Not right

indicators.note: R, for right, is dropped from the word for alarm

parts.note: fright means sudden alarm

explanation.surface: Is aggressive behaviour wrongly causing panic?
explanation.definitionFit: A fight is a violent physical struggle, an aggressive act.

clue.text: Buy bag containing tea

indicators.note: the word for bag holds the tea inside it

parts.note: a purse is a small bag for money
cha is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: Purchasing a bag with tea inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA (also char) is old British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun a purchase is a thing bought, a buy, so the two match.

clue.text: Cafe isn't often brewing potentially hot drink

indicators.note: brewing stirs things up, so these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A café rarely makes something that could be a hot drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Granules dissolved in hot water make a quick cup, so it may become a hot beverage.

clue.text: Female left oil installation, heading north

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading from the bottom up

parts.note: an oil rig drills at sea

explanation.surface: A woman leaves an oil rig, travelling north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading north' turns LRIG upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl is a young female person, the noun matching the noun.

clue.text: Piano work, music youngsters like?

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
op, short for opus, is a numbered musical work

explanation.surface: A piece written for the piano, the kind of thing young people enjoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop music is the popular chart style aimed largely at young listeners, so the question mark marks a definition by description.

clue.text: Ape a man of the cloth

definitions.meaning: apes belong to the order of mammals with monkeys and humans

explanation.surface: To imitate a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' looks like a verb, mimic, but it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Apes belong to the mammal order of that name, and the title is held by the senior archbishop of a country, such as the Primate of All England.

clue.text: Forty days and nights in Paraguay's borders? That's quite enough!

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
only the outside letters of the country's name are taken

parts.note: Lent lasts forty days, recalling Christ's forty days and nights in the wilderness

explanation.surface: Six weeks in South America would be more than enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'borders' gives P and Y from Paraguay's; the 's is ignored, with 'in' putting LENT between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty means an ample amount, all that is needed.

clue.text: Fury as old car fails to start

indicators.note: the word for the old car loses its opening letter, as a car might fail to start

parts.note: a banger is British slang for a battered old car

explanation.surface: Someone is furious because their old car won't start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails to start' removes the B of BANGER, British slang for a clapped-out car.
explanation.definitionFit: Fury is extreme rage, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Sycophantic knight, we hear, horrid

indicators.note: signals that the title for a knight is taken by its sound, giving a near-twin spelling

parts.note: a knight is addressed by the title Sir
vile means horrid, nasty

explanation.surface: A fawning knight, people say, is a horrible man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns SIR into the sound SER, which joined to VILE gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Servile behaviour is slavishly obsequious, the same fawning flattery as sycophancy.

clue.text: What leaderless school must do to make progress

definitions.meaning: a school with no headteacher needs to acquire one, taking the phrase literally
to advance or succeed in life or work

explanation.surface: A school without a leader must do something in order to improve.
explanation.walkthrough: The first part is read literally: the school needs to obtain a head teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for advancing in a career or life is to pull in front of others, an everyday phrase.

clue.text: Don't eat quickly

definitions.meaning: to go without food, as for religious observance

explanation.surface: An instruction not to bolt your food.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is abstaining from food, the other is the adverb meaning rapidly; both are standard dictionary senses.

clue.text: Share out proceeds from this independent cinema

indicators.note: the answer is what results from mixing up the two words, and proceeds also suggests box-office takings

explanation.surface: A small picture house splits its takings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'proceeds from this' rearranges SHARE OUT; 'out' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An art house is a small cinema showing independent and foreign films.

clue.text: Strongly criticise country's Christmas fare?

parts.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly
Turkey is the country; the 's stands for 'is', a link

explanation.surface: Attacking a nation's festive dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional British Christmas dinner centres on a cooked bird, so the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: Like the M25? Part gets spoken about

indicators.note: the word for spoken goes around the word for part

parts.note: oral means spoken
a bit is a part

explanation.surface: A section of a motorway attracts gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: The M25 is London's ring motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: The M25 circles London, so it is a ring road, described by this adjective of circling.

clue.text: Sound of bell in church makes you feel embarrassed

indicators.note: the bell's sound goes inside the church letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a bell's sound is its ring

explanation.surface: A bell pealing in church makes someone squirm.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe is to wince or shrink inwardly with awkwardness or shame.

clue.text: Stock of wine merchant talked about

indicators.note: the word for merchant is taken as it sounds when said out loud

parts.note: a seller is a merchant

explanation.surface: A wine merchant's supplies are being discussed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellar is a collection of wines kept by a person or restaurant.

clue.text: Cuts of meat reduced in butchers' shops for a start

indicators.note: the opening letters of each of the four words are taken

explanation.surface: Joints of meat on sale cheaply at the butcher's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a start' takes the first letters of 'reduced in butchers' shops'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare ribs and rib of beef are standard butchers' cuts, so this is an example plural.

clue.text: Reach old ruined town in NW England

indicators.note: ruined letters are broken up and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Arriving at an old, derelict town in the north-west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges REACH plus OLD. ROCHDALE is a Lancashire mill town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: Rochdale is a town in Greater Manchester, in the north-west of England.

clue.text: A mostly uninteresting time for grown-up

indicators.note: the word for uninteresting loses its final letter

parts.note: dull means uninteresting

explanation.surface: A rather boring period for a grown-up.
explanation.definitionFit: An adult is a fully grown person, the same as a grown-up.

clue.text: Catch one's breath as general practitioner comes round

indicators.note: the doctor's letters go round the little word

parts.note: GP is the abbreviation for a general practitioner, a family doctor

explanation.surface: A patient gasps as the doctor arrives on a visit.
explanation.definitionFit: To gasp is to draw in breath sharply, as in shock.

clue.text: Less than 50%? Absolutely right

definitions.meaning: read literally, a share that does not reach a half
British exclamation of emphatic agreement, like 'and how!'

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether a figure is under fifty per cent and is told emphatically yes.
explanation.walkthrough: As an exclamation, NOT HALF is British slang for very much so.
explanation.definitionFit: The British retort means very much indeed, an emphatic yes, the sense of agreeing wholeheartedly.

clue.text: Expected almost everyone to attend American university

indicators.note: the shortened word goes alongside, accompanying the other pieces

parts.note: US stands for the United States, so American

indicators.note: the word for everyone loses its final letter, so it is nearly complete

parts.note: all means everyone

explanation.surface: Everyone was expected at an American university.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the shortened word first, but 'to attend' means it accompanies the American university, so it goes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something usual is what is normally expected, an adjective synonym.

clue.text: Three lakes containing fish

indicators.note: the words hold the answer within them

explanation.surface: A trio of lakes that hold fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'containing' signals the letters running across 'thrEE Lakes'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a snake-like fish, an example of the class.

clue.text: TV compere now introduces member of the royal family

indicators.note: the word for now comes first, leading into the royal piece

parts.note: the present means now, the current time
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A television host is now introducing one of the royals.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A presenter hosts a television programme, which is what a compere does.
